commentary: The book stayed all-cash today, which is exactly right after last week's two losses -- and today gave a good reminder why patience pays. Chip stocks sold off hard on news of a strong new Chinese AI model, oil jumped on rising Middle East tension, and Netflix's earnings drop dragged the broader market down even though the S&P is still in a healthy long-term uptrend. Nothing on my watchlist actually needed a decision today: AMD hit my price level but not my real condition (I want to see it confirm strength after next week's AI event, not just dip into support), and every other name is either extended after a huge run or waiting on its own earnings date. The one wrinkle worth knowing about: a well-reasoned UnitedHealth trade I researched today got blocked by what looks like a technical glitch rather than a real problem with the idea, so I've kept it on the watchlist instead of letting it quietly vanish. Two names got fresh attention tonight -- Abbott, which is showing the first real signs of the stock confirming what management said on today's earnings call, and Boston Scientific, where company insiders have quietly bought over half a million dollars of stock with their own money even as the shares sit near a two-year low. Bottom line: still watching, still patient, still all cash, and that is the strategy working, not stalling.

closed_trades.thesis: HPE is the most valuation-protected way to own the AI-server/networking buildout in a tape where reaccelerating inflation (CPI 4.27%) and a rising 10-year (4.56%) are punishing rich multiples. It trades at just ~12.2x forward earnings and 1.67x sales - the cheapest in the server group - after a record fiscal Q2 and the completed Juniper acquisition, which adds a scaled networking franchise. Sell-side has responded with a +40.5% 30-day upward EPS revision, yet the stock is consolidating (1m +1.4%) and sits 23.8% below its 52-week high, so estimates are rising while price has not re-rated. The same SMCI collapse (-29%) that helps Dell consolidates enterprise AI-server demand toward HPE as customers de-risk suppliers. With the last print already behind it (38 days ago) and no earnings inside the 40-day window, this is a clean cheap-re-rating swing.

Dell is the best risk/reward in an extended AI-server complex: it pairs elite momentum (+143% 3m, +202% 6m) with the cheapest valuation in the group (forward P/E ~20.9, P/S 2.2) and a constructive entry, having pulled back only 2.2% from its 20-day high while sitting 4.1% off its 52-week high near a buy point. The 29% collapse in Super Micro is a direct tailwind, consolidating enterprise/AI-server share toward Dell as customers de-risk suppliers. Q1 fundamentals (revenue $23.4B, net income $965M) confirm profitable scale, and the current tape ('Dell Stock Nears Buy Point') shows institutional demand building. With no earnings until 9/3, a 45-day swing captures the momentum leg without event risk.

improvements.note: Weekly self-review: Last Friday's stated change was to get the insider Form-4 feed pre-classified into sponsor/10b5-1 vs. discretionary officer transactions instead of handing me hundreds of noisy rows -- that fix landed and it worked: tonight's insider_activity block gave clean, directly actionable signals (BSX bullish_cluster_buying, 3 officers buying $554K with zero sells; ZS notable_discretionary_selling), a real improvement over last week's noise. The trading result this week was rougher: my only two closed trades, DELL and HPE, both lost (-$135 and -$45, 0% win rate, avg R -0.98), and with only 2 closed trades this is anecdote-level evidence per my own sample-size rules -- I am not inventing hard rules from it, but the pattern is worth naming honestly. Both losses shared the same demand_driver (hyperscaler_server_capex/servers_hardware) dressed up as two separate theses when the actual catalyst language ('SMCI collapse consolidates AI-server share') was nearly identical -- bad reasoning (thin diversification), not bad data, and it is exactly the clustering the system's theme-risk cap now exists to prevent. HPE's exit was graded process_fail: I closed it at $46.08 without its $43.75 stop being hit and without a clearly named invalidator firing -- conviction cracked, not thesis broken, which is the discretionary-exit mistake I need to stop making. What I got right: after those two losses on 7/15, the book stayed disciplined and all-cash through the rest of the week, including declining a real-looking AMD dip-buy today because my own stated trigger condition (post-event confirmation) was not actually met. A new engineering issue surfaced tonight -- a validator-clean UNH proposal was rejected at execution with 'insufficient cash' on a 100%-cash account, which needs an engineering look, not a reasoning fix. The one change for next week: before any discretionary SELL_TO_CLOSE that isn't a stop or horizon exit, I will name the specific thesis_invalidator that actually fired in the sell thesis itself -- if none of the three stated invalidators fired, the move is to hold or trim with sell_fraction, not a full discretionary close.

** The deterministic trigger check fired on AMD purely because the *price* touched the parsed $500 level, but my published `would_buy_at` was a compound condition — *post-event* confirmation plus a 50-DMA reclaim, explicitly excluding a pre-event dip. The result is a full event-driven run spun up for a setup that was never actually live, five days before its own catalyst. The trigger parser could be materially sharper if it also parsed an *event/date gate* from the trigger text (e.g. "after 7/22-23") and suppressed or down-weighted the alert until that date passes, rather than firing on the price alone. That would save event-driven runs for triggers whose *conditions*, not just prices, are met — reducing exactly this kind of "premature trigger" cycle.

** The single highest-value fix this run is upstream of my judgment: the orchestrator handed me a portfolio reading `$0 equity / $0 cash / no positions` with no `data_quality` or `stale_data_notice` flag raised, even though the trade history mathematically implies ~$9,820 should exist. A cheap deterministic guard — "if broker equity is ~$0 but closed-trade math implies non-trivial cash, flag `broker_sync_suspect` and set `allows_new_buys: false` with a reason" — would prevent a future run from being invited to trade (this was even a trigger-driven run) against an account it cannot possibly fund, and would save me from spending the cycle diagnosing broker plumbing instead of setups. Separately, the watchlist trigger checker should parse the *qualitative* half of `would_buy_at` (here, "confirmed positive reaction to the 7/22-23 event... not a bounce off today's low") rather than only the first dollar figure, so it stops firing event-driven runs on price alone before the event has occurred.

Daily study session produced no machine-readable lesson - prompt/parse needs attention.
** Two concrete data defects cost me real research time and nearly cost me a bad trade.

`gap_analysis` reports a gap's size, direction, and whether it later filled, but not how the session actually closed relative to its open — so UNH shows an unfilled +7.4% gap while `pct_change_1d` is only +1.16%, meaning most of the pop was sold intraday, and I had to infer that from two fields that don't reconcile on their face. A `close_vs_open_pct` (or an `intraday_fade` flag) on the gap object would let an evening review distinguish a *held* gap from a *faded* one, which is the entire difference between a real drift setup and a failed print — precisely the call I had to hedge on UNH tonight. Secondary: `momentum_health` was absent from this bundle entirely (not even `unknown`), and `position_histories` was `skipped`, so two documented inputs to the regime read were silently missing rather than explicitly null.

The relay bundle's intraday price for AMD (last_close $548.81, +2.7%) diverged meaningfully from independently-verified real-time coverage ($566.73, +6.05%) even though data_quality reported the bundle as only 0.5h old - on a day with a fast, catalyst-driven intraday move, a 0.5h-old snapshot for a non-focus scan name can already be stale enough to make a trigger look unconfirmed when live volume/price may have since caught up; worth having the gather step timestamp each ticker's price pull individually (not just the bundle as a whole) so I can weight staleness per-name rather than assuming uniform freshness across 50+ scanned tickers.
